title: Centre of a split reductive group from the root lattice
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] and let $H$ be a reductive affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme], meaning smooth, connected and of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Use the torus and root conventions of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subset H$, put $X=X^*(T)$, let $\Phi\subset X$ be the roots, and put $L=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbf Z\alpha$. For a commutative $F$-algebra $A$, let $Z(H)(A)$ consist of those elements of $H(A)$ that commute with every element of $H(A')$ after every commutative $A$-algebra extension $A'$. Then $Z(H)$ is the closed subgroup scheme $\bigcap_{\alpha\in\Phi}\ker(\alpha:T\to\mathbf G_m)$ of $T$ and there is a group-scheme isomorphism $$Z(H)\simeq D_F(X/L)=\operatorname{Spec}F[X/L].$$ Here $F[M]$ is the group algebra with basis $e_m$ for $m\in M$, multiplication $e_me_n=e_{m+n}$, coproduct $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$, counit $e_m\mapsto1$, and antipode $e_m\mapsto e_{-m}$; its spectrum is as in [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Under this isomorphism restriction of characters $X^*(T)\to X^*(Z(H))$ is the quotient map $X\to X/L$. The intersection and isomorphism are scheme-theoretic, including on nonreduced test algebras.

source.place: Propositions 21.7 and 21.8, printed p.427; root weights in paragraph 21.1, printed p.425.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change], the centre functor in the statement is a closed subgroup scheme $Z\subseteq H$. Its points centralize $T$ after every scalar extension. Applying [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer] over the already algebraically closed field $F$ gives $Z\subseteq T$ scheme-theoretically. Put $N=\ker(\operatorname{Ad}:H\to\operatorname{GL}(\operatorname{Lie}H))$. For a central point $z\in Z(A)$, conjugation by $z$ is the identity morphism of $H_A$, since it is the identity on points over every $A$-algebra. Its differential at the identity is therefore the identity, so $z\in N(A)$. Thus $Z\subseteq N\cap T$.

source.place: Proposition 21.7, printed p.427, first two sentences of proof; explicit differentiation over each test algebra.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] for the $T$-weight decomposition $\operatorname{Lie}H=\operatorname{Lie}T\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak h_\alpha$, where each $\mathfrak h_\alpha$ is one-dimensional. For every $F$-algebra $A$ and $t\in T(A)$, the operator $\operatorname{Ad}(t)$ is the identity on $\operatorname{Lie}T\otimes_F A$ and multiplication by $\alpha(t)$ on $\mathfrak h_\alpha\otimes_F A$. Choosing a nonzero basis vector in each root space shows that this operator is the identity exactly when every $\alpha(t)=1$; this remains true when $A$ has nilpotents. Hence $N\cap T=K:=\bigcap_{\alpha\in\Phi}\ker\alpha$ as subgroup functors. It is closed: in the affine torus impose the finitely many equations $\alpha-1=0$, using the affine quotient-ring description in [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Therefore the preceding step gives $Z\subseteq K$.

source.place: Paragraph 21.1, printed p.425, and Proposition 21.8, printed p.427, first displayed equality; weight scalars are characters, not differentials.

proof.text: The closed subgroup $K$ of the split torus is isomorphic to $D_F(M)$ for some finitely generated abelian $M$, by [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable]. Apply [lem-sfb-adjoint-kernel-central-quotient-unipotent] to the smooth connected affine finite-type group $H$, obtaining $q:N\to U\subseteq\mathcal U_{n,F}$ with kernel $Z$. The composite $D_F(M)\simeq K\hookrightarrow N\xrightarrow{q}U$ is trivial by [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-to-unipotent-trivial]. Thus every $K(A)$-point lies in $\ker q(A)=Z(A)$, for every $F$-algebra $A$. Together with $Z\subseteq K$, this proves $Z=K$ as closed subgroup schemes. Neither $K$ nor $U$ has been assumed smooth.

source.place: Proposition 21.7, printed p.427, last two sentences, using 14.23 and 14.18(b).

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality], the split torus has its natural evaluation identification $T\simeq D_F(X)$. A point of $D_F(X)$ over any $F$-algebra $A$ is an algebra map $F[X]\to A$, equivalently a group homomorphism $h:X\to A^\times$: send $x$ to the image of $e_x$, which is a unit with inverse the image of $e_{-x}$; conversely extend $h$ $F$-linearly. This is the affine-spectrum correspondence of [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Under evaluation, $h(x)=x(t)$ for $t\in T(A)$. Such an $h$ belongs to $K(A)$ exactly when $h(\alpha)=1$ for every root. Since $L$ consists of integral sums of roots, this is equivalent to $h(l)=1$ for every $l\in L$. The quotient-group property then gives a unique homomorphism $\bar h:X/L\to A^\times$ with $h=\bar h\circ(X\to X/L)$. This bijection is natural in $A$ and respects multiplication. Explicitly its inclusion into $T$ is induced contravariantly by the Hopf map $F[X]\to F[X/L]$, $e_x\mapsto e_{[x]}$; it commutes with coproduct, counit and antipode on each basis element. The universal $K$-point over its coordinate algebra factors as just described and gives a map $K\to D_F(X/L)$. Conversely the universal character $X/L\to F[X/L]^\times$, composed with $X\to X/L$, gives $D_F(X/L)\to K$. The two composites are identities because their homomorphisms on $X$, respectively $X/L$, are identities. Thus $K\simeq D_F(X/L)$ as group schemes by the affine-spectrum correspondence.

source.place: Proposition 21.8, printed p.427; Theorem 12.9(a),(b), pp.233--234. Explicit functor-of-points version of the character quotient.

proof.text: The quotient $X/L$ is finitely generated since $X$ is the character group of a split torus. The character identification $X^*(D_F(X/L))=X/L$ and its naturality in [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality] identify pullback along the inclusion of the preceding step with $x\mapsto[x]$: the character $x$ evaluates on $\bar h$ as $\bar h([x])$. Replacing $K$ by $Z$ proves the asserted restriction formula. All constructions and inverse maps above used arbitrary commutative $F$-algebras, so the assertion includes nonreduced algebras. If $\Phi$ is empty, then $L=0$, $K=T$, and the same argument gives $Z(H)=T$; no root or positive-rank case was excluded.

source.place: Proposition 21.8, printed p.427, character quotient and its natural map; empty-root case included.

This is valid on nonreduced test algebras, so it gets SL_2 in char 2 (μ_2) right; I also checked GL_n, PGL_2 and the empty-root case.
